title: Cancel Opposite-Case Neighbours
statement:
You get a string s of English letters in upper and lower case. Two neighbouring characters cancel when they are the same letter in different case, like "q" next to "Q" (in either order). Both are removed and the pieces on either side join up, which can create a new cancelling pair.

Keep cancelling until no pair is left and return what remains. The result is the same whichever pair you cancel first. It may be the empty string. Two equal characters in the same case, like "aa", do not cancel.

examples.why: "qQ" cancels, which brings "p" and "P" together; they cancel too.
Same letter in the same case does not cancel, and "a" and "B" are different letters.
The middle "mM" cancels, leaving "mM", which cancels as well.

hints: Cancelling is like an undo: the newest kept character is the one a new character can cancel with. Which data structure keeps the newest item on top?
Read left to right and keep the characters that survived so far on a stack.
For each character, if the top of the stack is the same letter in the other case, pop it; otherwise push the character. The stack is the answer.

explain.intuition:
Rescanning the string after every removal is slow: each pass may remove only one pair. Notice that a new character can only ever cancel with the last surviving character before it. Everything older is hidden behind that one.

That is exactly a stack. Push characters as you read them; when the next character cancels with the top, pop instead of pushing. Popping can expose an older character, which the following character may cancel with in turn. Same idea as matching brackets, where "a" and "A" are an opening and closing pair that can come in either order.
steps: For each character c: if the stack is not empty and its top t satisfies t !== c and t.toLowerCase() === c.toLowerCase(), pop.
Join the stack into a string and return it.
pitfalls: Cancelling identical characters too: "aa" must stay. The case has to differ.
Only scanning once without a stack, which misses pairs created by earlier removals, like in "pqQPr".
Building the answer with repeated string slicing, which makes every removal O(n).

solutions.title: Rescan until nothing cancels
solutions.idea: Find the first cancelling pair, cut it out, and repeat until a full pass finds none.

solutions.title: Stack of survivors
solutions.idea: A new character can only cancel with the latest survivor, so keep survivors on a stack and pop on a match.

followups: Do it in place on a character array with O(1) extra space. (Hint: the write index acts as the stack top.)
Only lowercase-then-uppercase ("aA") cancels, not "Aa". Does the stack approach still work?
